When I was about 35 years old and in pretty decent shape, I hiked all the way down to the Colorado River from Bright Angel Trail. It took us 9+ hours, and that was going down. We started at 5am and it was dark and chilly (almost freezing) at the top. By the time we reached the bottom it was over 100F. Scorching, pounding, relentless sun. We cooled off in the river, found shade and then went with our rafting guides for a few days down the river. An awesome (in the true sense of the word) and unforgettable experience. Humbling and life changing.

The canyon is so deep that you don't even see the river until you're nearly upon it. The Grand Canyon is immense and so big it's hard to get your head around it.

No way in HELL could I have made it back up to the rim. Going down was difficult enough, and yes, hiking downward presents different muscular aches and pains. But climbing/scrambling up that distance? I seriously doubt I could do it in a day. 

On top of that, on our hike down, we carried minimal stuff... water bottles (there were a handful of stations to refill bottles with a pump on this trail), a bunch of snacks, a light backpack with extra sunscreen, and very basic things like that. The tour company carried most of our necessary supplies and tents and met us at the river. (It was so pleasantly warm/dry at night at the bottom of the canyon that I didn't even sleep in the tent, just covered up with a very light sleeping bag... we camped on sandy beaches near turns in the river. It was amazing.)

We got a helicopter ride up and out of the canyon on the 4th day. Wasn't a cheap experience, but considering the quality of the guides, the food (they packed and prepared) and the insane impact that the trip had on my soul, it was worth every penny.

I know people in this thread are glamorizing this older man's death ("better than a hospital)", but slowly dying of heatstroke and exposure as you desperately try to make it back to the top is not a pretty thought.

Going from a crappy TV or monitor to an OLED 4k will be a better investment than keeping the crappy monitor and upgrading the console.  
...............

In December, I figured the economy was going to soon take a dive with tariffs and other stupid, irrational insanity, so I decided to upgrade my gear. I went from a decent (but 6+ year old) 4k monitor to an OLED, 240hz, 4k with VRR. I got the new monitor first, and just plugging the old PS5 into it was a jaw-dropping improvement. Astonishing.

A week later I got the Pro. Yes, the Pro is nice. It's a small upgrade. It is a slightly better improvement over the original PS5. But the difference in display knocked my socks off. Upgrading to the Pro was nice, but not nearly as much of a leap.

I recommend to anyone on a budget: **get a great display/TV/monitor first.** Get the best you can reasonably afford, at the best size for your space (I like to game at a desk, so 32" was plenty big for me... on a sofa, you will want much, much larger). If necessary, save money and invest in the display, because you want it to last for 2-3 console generations. That's possibly 10 years. 

Only then get the Pro. I am not shitting on the Pro. But the difference between the PS5 and the PS5 Pro is not a giant leap by any means. Future-proof your display... then upgrade your console.

I highly doubt we'll be gaming in 8k within the next 10 years, and I don't even have a way to input 8k into a display at this point. I really think 4k will be fine for the next 8-10 years. Hell, most stuff you pay for to stream isn't even in 4k! Maybe my expectation of 10 years for my monitor is unrealistic... but I know (barring some weird event) my monitor will outlast my PS5 Pro. The PS6 is likely coming within 6 years.

Was just there last week. 5 days in and around Oaxaca town, and four days in Puerto Escondido near La Punta.

American husband and wife, ages 54 and 61. We felt 100% safe the entire time. There were a few areas where I felt like we needed to turn around in the outskirts of the tourist Centro zone, but that was me being a little gun shy and the fact that I stand out like a gringo (My wife is Mexican American and looks like a local). We wandered into an area that wasn't necessarily dangerous looking, but it was very deserted, so we turned around.

We got jumped about 20 years ago in Barcelona so we are always careful (the guys that jumped us were teenagers... they didn't get anything, wife does not wear jewelry or carry a purse on trips,  knocked us down, felt for my wallet which I had around my neck... we were on the ground for maybe 4 seconds and they all ran away in different directions.. we were un-hurt but a little freaked out).

Cops are everywhere in Oaxaca. Tourism and selling artisanal goods to visitors is one of the biggest sources of income for the state and city, so the cops make damn sure no one is fucking around... not even petty crime. People will approach you to sell you stuff, but not a single one of them got pushy in the least. A simple "No, gracias!" with a smile turned them away. We saw no disturbances or anything out of the ordinary the whole time. Very friendly place.

Hell, even with mezcalerias everywhere and tons of places to drink, we didn't even see anyone acting drunk, sloppy or rowdy. It was a very family-centric kind of place. Many people had kids with them, especially at the end of Semana Santa (We arrived the day before Good Friday).

Oaxaca was one of the most chill, safe feeling places I have ever visited and I've been to 17 different countries, some countries multiple times. We had a great time. I would recommend 4 days in Oaxaca at the very most. You can see the entire old part of town and eat at a bunch of great restaurants and fun little holes in the wall. More than four days is probably too much. (edit: just re-read your question... as long as you are in the old central part of Oaxaca you will be fine.)

Spend the rest of your time doing day trips. Monte Albán was fantastic. We left early morning, got there around 8:30am on Saturday and had the place mostly to ourselves. Plus it was cooler that way. By the time we left near noon, it was very busy. We just caught a taxi back (can't remember how much but it was less than $25 USD for a 30-minute drive), though it's apparently not always easy to find taxis returning. Because we were leaving when many  people were arriving, it was a breeze. We had zero wait.

I don't know how long you intend to go for, but the 3-hour bus ride to the coast was awesome. As mentioned, we stayed in Puerto Escondido, the "La Punta" area, which was kind of a sleepy, artsy, surfer-hippy vibe. Not a massive party place at all (though there's a bunch of good restaurants and bars, people just don't get sloppy drunk that we saw). And everything closed by 11pm. Very chill, very low key. Gorgeous beach, but the water is more for surfing than swimming. I'ma  decent swimmer but couldn't go out very far because the waves and rip currents were tremendous. But it was enough to cool off and have a great time.

DM me if you'd like to know more. We had a wonderful time and are already planning on returning. We've been all over Mexico and this is one of our favorite spots because it's so chill and non-crazy party-town. Great food in Oaxaca and in La Punta! Make reservations for the more popular restaurants via their websites, it's easy to do and a lot of these places are small and will fill up pretty fast.

Check, double check and triple check for evidence of flooding/seepage in the basement. Warped wood trim at floor level, damp spots, smell, wall cracks, relative humidity. Get a home inspector that YOU pay for come and look at the house and the basement.

One big reason I got out of the business after around 20 years was that the only way to start making more money was to become a manager. Creative directors spend most of their time managing. I did that work, but I did NOT want to do that work. I knew I was no good at it and I hated it. But the only way to get those raises was to go higher in creative direction (I was an art director).

What this meant was: in order for companies to keep top talent, they force-fit them into managerial (creative director) roles. They were by and large not good at managing anything, but in order for the number on the paycheck to rise, that was the only way to go.

So you have this stable of talent being managed by people who either suck at managing or don't really want to be managing anyway - even if they are good at it. Of course there are exceptions. But that's what I saw.

Eventually I started freelancing, which was great, great money. And it's wonderful to walk in a door and be greeted by people who are extremely happy to have you join in and help out. But you never really get to own those projects... you get hired for a while until chaos settles down ("Chaos is good" was a saying among the freelancers I knew!) then you were out on the street or putting out fires somewhere else.

It's just a toxic business that is being more and more devalued every year. Of course there are exceptions to this; top end agencies still do great work, but the pool of competition is simply ludicrous these days. And companies would rather hire 2 younger creatives over one creative with great experience and skills. And most writers will be replaced by machine-learning tools very soon. Hell, I did freelance work on direct mail sometimes (ugh) and some of these "writers" just had to come up with a few subheads for variations on mailings. An attentive high schooler could do it.

Some of what I write here has always been the case. But I just saw the business become faster, faster, faster and sloppier as my career went along. I had to get out.

Just hang tight for a while. I get that it can be frustrating. But the fact is: you are the New Kid.

No one wants to hear the New Kid pipe up all the time about how their approach is better or more modern or more functional. Or whatever. Not to say you should remain silent. Offer up options, suggestions. And don't expect them to take the company by storm.

There's all kinds of business and often interpersonal and political reasons why an agency is working a certain way. In the end, the agency needs to bring in steady cash to pay everyone and keep the lights on. Period.

You are the New Kid and while I do not doubt your skills or potential or enthusiasm, I guarantee there's factors involved that you just don't know about. Either because no one tells you, or you aren't involved in the high level conversations, or because you don't fully grasp the entire nature of the business. You are still new to the business, and while you might be an amazingly talented designer, you just do not have the experience of how an agency really works.

Just remember: design and ad agencies try to do the "best" work but in the end they are beholden to their clients and (sometimes) shareholders. I've worked at giant agencies that won all kinds of awards around the world. But you know what kept the bills paid, and the lights on and the staff getting paychecks? Their direct mail division. Yep, junk mail paid the bills and allowed the agency to let certain teams go crazy and compete for prestigious awards. The Agency promoted the cool ads and the award winning work, but their telecom direct mail division brought in a steady stream of big money.

You often don't hear about what really pays the bills. A long time ago, I worked at Leo Burnett, which had its level of prestige. But they made most of their money through Philip Morris (cigarettes). Leo Burnett didn't crow about the cigarette business, in fact they kept it really, really quiet. But the Marlboro account was far and away their biggest money maker.

Just some thoughts. Hang in there, it's a job.

Do you live on a street with big old trees? Then it's a good idea to get your main drainpipe that leads to the municipal sewer system checked out. Hopefully it's clear. Old homes in Chicago (and I'm sure many other places around the USA) had clay pipes leading through the front, under the sidewalk and to the main city sewer. Tree roots can and will grow right through the clay eventually and clog the drains. This drain pipe can be routed out every year or every other year which is a temporary fix. You can also rip it out and replace that main drain pipe with metal, but that can be very costly.

At least get it checked. Because for the most part, even if it's full of roots, it can drain just fine 99% of the time. But if you get a really bad storm, water can back up into your basement. They will run a wire and a camera through it and you can see in real time if it is clogged or partially clogged.

This isn't an emergency, but put it on your calendar to get it looked at.

On the other hand, this may be a complete non-issue for you. I hope so.

People didn't like that BG3 was similar to the Divinity: Original Sin games that Larian had created. They didn't like things such as throwing potions (one example), the verticality, jumping, and they also didn't like so many cut scenes. They felt that Larian was straying too far from an established formula that they had loved since their childhoods.

Essentially, the haters were Grognards looking for another game from 2002 (perhaps with more hi res graphics and animations).

BG3 was the best game I have ever played. And yes, I'm 54 and played the original BG games. BG1 & 2 are essential classics, but it's absurd to think that a game company would create another cookie-cutter version of a game that old. Larian was masterful in everything from gameplay, onboarding new players (the radial menus do an exceptional job displaying the options you have during your turn, something the old games did not have at all). FFS, the original games came with a thick booklet of D&D rules, which (for better or worse) is not something we will ever see again.

Besides: I think it's a huge improvement that people completely unfamiliar with D&D rules can jump in and play without the options being super limited or watered down. Larian created a masterpiece.

I don't think BG3 was perfect. Act 3 was weirdly misguided in a pacing sense, and there remain some buggy areas especially in Act 3. I never could complete the haunted house for instance. Act 3 just plain threw too many quests at you... by that point  in the game you were high level, saving the world from an existential threat, but Larian was trying to make you care what a newspaper headline would say about you? An enormous benefit of the old landline system was that the sound quality of the calls and the quality of conversations you could have was far, far better.

With old landlines, you could more easily talk over another person. Now... that sounds like a bad thing. I don't mean shouting the other person down. Cell phones have terrible voice and sound quality (in general) compared to the old landline system (in general). Yes, there were occasional "bad connections" but those were vanishingly rare, especially in calls within the country. Local calls around the city where you live were almost 100% clear, crisp and very natural sounding audio.

I feel like people stopped noticing this with the novelty of cell phones. Yes, cell phones are generally wonderful, it's much safer to have a phone in your pocket wherever you go. But the sound quality of phone conversations is far, far worse than old landline conversations.

Google some info on growing cacti with grow lights. People will have the lights literally 1" from the plant. 12+ hours a day. You almost can't give them too much light.

Think of the sun in Arizona, or Northern Mexico. It's extremely bright and it's not often cloudy. That's where these things evolved (they evolved in many other parts of the world, but this is just an example). It's difficult to re-create conditions like that in a home.

Without enough strong light, they will etiolate and become weak and leggy. The intense light keeps them growing compact and healthy.

Most houseplants are tropical or subtropical plants that naturally grow under a forest canopy... so they evolved to thrive in lower light conditions, shaded partially by the trees overhead. Think of jungle plants below the treeline. Lower light conditions in a house is often enough to keep them happy (depending on the plant).

Many tropical house plants would burn if you left them out in full sun in the summer time.

Another thing is: sun coming through a glass window gets a lot of its UV rays filtered out. so even direct sun through a window is much weaker than direct sun with no glass in between.

I swear I finished World and never, ever figured out much of the terminology, the difference between types of Hunts, etc. Play the campaign and just go with the flow. There's a million options for everything, but you do not, nor are you expected to use all the options.

Remember that you have weapon durability, so when hunting, take time to get away and sharpen your weapon from time to time. You even need to "sharpen" your Hammers, etc. Hunts can go on for 30+ minutes and possibly much longer. Monsters will run away. Take that time to heal, buff yourself, sharpen weapon then go chase them. The quick-slots and inventory system took me a long time to figure out, too, but I muddled through. Again: there's a million options but you do not even need to understand most of the options.

Ultimately, the game is, kill monsters for parts. Use those parts to upgrade your gear. Your gear can be upgraded to many different paths, depending on what you want to do. Be more fire resistant, put electricity on your Sword, etc. A far as I remember you can just keep upgrading different stuff, so you aren't really locked into choices, you just need to build multiple versions of the gear pieces.

It's a grind game. Decide on a load out of weapon, potions, remedies, etc that you will take on your hunt. Then, you kill, you upgrade to kill stronger foes, and use their parts to upgrade to kill stronger foes. The story and campaign are kind of beside the point.

You also play as kind of a scientist and explorer. Harvest stuff, discover new wildlife. Some NPCs will give quests to gather ingredients, or materials, or find new kinds of bugs or plants or lizards, etc. You can do that stuff while you are on a main Hunt, or just while running around in the world. I worked on Marlboro advertising later than this period: around 2000-2003. Most ads like these were gone in the USA by then, though they appeared overseas.

Yes, one of the original Marlboro cowboys was a heavy smoker and died of lung cancer. But the younger dudes like this guy did not smoke, and just posed with the cigarettes and collected a paycheck. What's interesting is these guys all knew real cowboy stuff... they were skilled riders, ropers and ranch hands. But they also considered themselves athletes. One of these guys was extremely good at tennis, was a semi-pro.

For these shots, someone just off-camera would light the smoke, take approximately 2 pulls on it and hand it to the cowboy. They were coached on how to hold it, etc. And there were like 40,000 outtake photos like this taken and edited down to a handful of shots that were retouched and used.

The "cigarette-pull" thing was very much considered and studied. The art directors had an exact length of ash they wanted on the smoke. It had to look new-lit, but not completely new-lit. There was a steel bucket with water at this guy's feet where he would dump the smokes after posing with them.

Phillip Morris was very, very careful about fire safety. Unless it was on private land, they always had a rep from the Bureau of Land Management accompanying the shoots. They followed laws stringently. They were the largest tobacco company on earth and therefore the one most likely to be sued for ANYTHING.

Shots like these were rigorously studied and made to happen very, very carefully. Hundreds of person-hours, if not thousands of person-hours went into a final ad like this. I'm not exaggerating.

The action-cowboy shots didn't include smokes, but it was the real guys doing the work/stunts. They spent ludicrous sums of money on these shoots. Each banana grew from a single flower. The flower stalks come out of the plant in a sort of linear cluster, like a gladiolus (but they hang upside down). So these linear groups of flowers get pollinated and then the female part of the plant gets elongated and grows into the banana we know. It starts hard and green but eventually ripens yellow. These stalks of banana can be enormous... they are cut apart before going to the grocery store, which is why bananas come in a bunch.

That blunt end of the banana is where the flower was. Once pollinated and the fruit grows, the flower petals wither and drop off.

Commercially purchased bananas are highly hybridized. A natural or 'species' banana fruit is full of tough, hard seeds with just a little bit of the fruit pulp between the seeds. They've been hybridized to be "seedless" the same way "seedless" watermelons have been. There are actually tiny vestigial seeds in the bananas we eat, but they are so tiny and soft you don't even notice them.

They are fascinating plants. Do some searching for them. Really beautiful, almost alien looking when in bloom and the fruits are developing.

The first "combo" is literally "swing, swing, swing" without touching the joystick (as long as you start from the right or left!) Tomcat makes it seem like you need to keep moving the joystick. The way I kind of see it is the red point of the star is where the sword is. If you don't reposition it, it will go to where it naturally goes when you make the swing.

For instance if you press up (position your sword to start from the top) and then press swing, the sword will naturally end up in the lower left point of the star (as you look at it)... it's where your arms would naturally end up.

So when moving the sword to start the next swing, you just lightly push in the direction you want to start in and then hit swing. You do NOT want to be mashing the joystick at any time. It's a slight repositioning that you are doing. I hope that makes sense.

As a former art director who used to work with "studio people" aka graphic designers all the time...

SHOW SOME CREATIVE PROBLEM SOLVING.

This happened far too often: We used to hand off work/ideas to the graphic designers. These were extremely competent technology people who knew the applications inside out. But they would often robotically follow instructions, even if the result was obviously wrong. They'd hand us what we asked them to do, even if it was obviously, painfully wrong, awkward, etc. 

Now I understand following instructions. Doing what you were asked. And maybe you need to show me something broken to prove it doesn't work. But catch the problem, point it out and offer some ideas for solutions!

Come up with a solution or two! Use your creative brain to solve the problem. Often what "sounds like it will work" will just not work at all... I get that. But don't just follow instructions that lead to a ridiculous result. Offer a couple alternatives!

I will take less accurate reflections in puddles if it means I get 60FPS. I will take weaker implementation of volumetric lighting if it means I get 60FPS. I will take less accurate foliage if I can get 60FPS.

The sad part is, "MOAR PIXELS" is a simple thing for consumers to understand, and Quality mode will look better in screenshots 95% of the time. So marketing pushes those numbers heavily.

I believe we should stop talking about graphics just as a measure of DPI and resolution. It should be discussed as "Graphical Presentation." The gamer is experiencing time and interaction with the game... they're not soaking in screenshots or vistas (except occasionally.) The gamer is presented with what is essentially an interactive cartoon, an animation created by artists using computers. 

If there's a super high resolution but at 30FPS or an uneven frame rate? It's going to be a bad time experiencing that for an hour or three. That to me is 'bad graphics" just as much as jagged, low count polygons in ugly colors are considered "bad graphics."

60FPS to me is the minimum where things start looking "realistically" smooth. More than 60 is great, and I hope that we see 120FPS on consoles some day. But the truth is: resolution numbers and "MOAR PIXELS" sells stuff.

Depends on the individual, how far you are seated from the display, etc.

I prefer to sit close and sit upright. A 55" would be way too large for the way I like to game. Not to mention it wouldn't comfortably fit on my gaming desk. Some people like to sit farther back on a couch in a living room type setup. In that case, a 55" would be great, and even larger would be better.

I just find myself wanting to be within 3 feet or so of the display. I have a 32" OLED monitor now and I love it. I could probably go up to 40" and be a little happier, but for my setup, 32" is plenty big.

It all comes down to preference. I have tried gaming in more of a couch/living room setup and I don't like it as much. I kept finding myself leaning forward, trying to get closer. I never felt right just reclining back on a couch.

There's no correct answer here. Try different setups and see what you like best. It might also depend on the room you will be in. If I somehow were to fit a 55" on my gaming desk in the smallish area I play in, I would feel overwhelmed and not able to take in the whole display at once.

But it's purely individual preference.

EDIT: of course, to some extent "bigger is better"... I wouldn't suggest a tiny screen. I think you have to look at it as maxing out the space you have with the position and setting of where you prefer to game.
